tip: Δεν θέλαμε (dhen thélame) takes the ongoing past form because wanting is a state, not an event: the not-wanting-to-leave lasted the whole trip.
Τους δύο (tus dhío) with 'the' in front means both; bare δύο (dhío) just counts: και για τους δύο (ke ya tus dhío) = for both of them.
Both verbs use the ongoing past form – ήταν (ítan) and οδηγούσαμε (odhighúsame) – setting the scene: the road stayed dirt, the driving stayed slow.
Μένω από (méno apó) is literally 'be left from' = to run out of: έμεινε από βενζίνη (émine apó venzíni) = it ran out of petrol.
Πριν plus a verb = before doing something: πριν φύγουμε (prin fíghume) = before we left.
Commands are negated with μην (min), not δεν (dhen): μην οδηγείς (min odhiyís) = don't ride. δεν states facts, μην forbids.
The ongoing past form covers repeated habits: κολυμπούσαμε (kolimbúsame) = we would swim.
Ένα βράδυ (éna vrádhi) plus the one-shot past pins a single finished event: φάγαμε (fághame) = we ate, that night and done.
Ενώ plus the ongoing past form = while: ενώ τρώγαμε (enó tróghame) = while we were eating.
Ξαφνικά (ksafniká) = suddenly, and it normally pairs with the one-shot past: νύχτωσε (níkhtose) = night fell, one sharp event.
The classic pair: ongoing past περπατούσαμε (perpatúsame) = we were walking, the backdrop; one-shot past είδαμε (ídhame) = we saw, the event cutting in.
Έλεγε (éleye) is the ongoing past for a habit: grandma told stories evening after evening. One single telling would be είπε (ípe).
Γνωρίζω (ghnorízo) = to know, but its one-shot past means met for the first time: γνωρίσαμε (ghnorísame) = we met, the knowing starting at one moment.
Με πήρε ο ύπνος (me píre o ípnos) is literally 'sleep took me' = I dozed off. Sleep is the doer here, you are the one it grabs.
Χορεύαμε (khorévame) stays in the ongoing past even with ένα βράδυ (éna vrádhi): the dancing went on for hours, and duration outweighs the one-night frame.
Αξίζει να (aksízi na) plus a verb = it's worth doing: αξίζει να πας (aksízi na pas) = it's worth going, with no word for 'it' needed.
Έχει κόσμο (ékhi kósmo) is literally 'it has people' = it's crowded; έχει with no subject covers weather too: έχει ζέστη (ékhi zésti) = it's hot.
The ending -άκι (-áki) makes things little: το καραβάκι (to karaváki) = the little boat.
Adverbs usually compare by adding -τερα: νωρίς (norís = early) becomes νωρίτερα (norítera = earlier), with no extra word for 'more'.
One verb covers both: χάνω (kháno) means lose and miss – μη χάσεις τη βόλτα (mi khásis ti vólta) = don't miss the walk.
Του χρόνου (tu khrónu) = next year – literally 'of the year'.
Μαζεύω λεφτά (mazévo leftá) = I save money – literally 'I gather money'.
Time is passed, not had: περάσαμε τέλεια (perásame télia) is literally 'we passed perfectly' – Greek's way of saying we had a great time.
Εδώ και τρεις μήνες (edhó ke tris mínes) is literally 'here and three months'; with the plain present ψάχνω (psákhno) it means I've been looking for three months now.
The 'me' comes before the verb: θα με πάρουν (tha me párun) = literally 'they'll me take'. In statements, short object words like με sit in front.
Stacking negatives is correct Greek: δεν με πήραν ποτέ (dhen me píran poté) is literally 'they didn't take me never', the standard way to say never.
Call back is call again: ξανα- (ksana = again) glues onto the verb, so θα ξαναπάρω (tha ksanapáro) = I'll call again; παίρνω πίσω (pérno píso) means take something back.
You make an application here: έκανα αίτηση (ékana étisi) = I applied. The lookalike εφαρμόζω (efarmózo) means implement, not apply for a job.
Where English uses 'to', Greek links two verbs with να: ελπίζω να βρω (elpízo na vro) = I hope to find; there is no plain 'to find' form to fall back on.
Dropping by is passing: να περάσω για μια κουβέντα (na peráso ya mia kuvénda) = literally 'to pass for a chat' – περνάω (pernáo) covers casual visits.
